issues: The thread is misleading as worded. It says P3P's idea is 'the same idea that person-proffered terms (IEEE 7012) and AI agents now revive, but with the site, not the person, stating the terms'. Read literally, this says IEEE 7012 has the site stating the terms, which is the reverse of the intended contrast. In P3P the site stated its policy; in IEEE 7012 the person proffers terms. Reworded.

Overstatement in the influence field: the post-mortem is called 'the standard account' of why P3P failed, and no source supports that. Changed to 'a detailed insider's account'. The rest of the field is now tied to the article's own findings. It found 'thousands of sites that had identical erroneous policies' traced 'to a Microsoft support website' after Internet Explorer made compact policies a cookie gate (FOUND). It also says that 'as of June 2012, no public enforcement actions have been taken based on P3P' (FOUND). The W3C 2018 obsoletion note repeats both points: the IE 'broad gate', sites choosing 'to copy general policies', and 'no enforcement action followed'.
The contribution understated her role: she chaired the W3C P3P Specification Working Group. The spec's Appendix 8 says the group was 'chaired by Lorrie Cranor (AT&T)', and her bio confirms it. Added.

fieldFixes.contribution: Cranor chaired the W3C working group that wrote P3P and was one of its authors; the standard (Recommendation, 16 April 2002) let websites publish their privacy practices in a machine-readable format for browsers to read on users' behalf. At Carnegie Mellon she directs the CyLab Usable Privacy and Security Laboratory and founded the Symposium On Usable Privacy and Security (SOUPS); with Aleecia McDonald she estimated in 2008 that reading the privacy policy of every new site an American visits would take about 244 hours a year. In 2012 she published a candid post-mortem of P3P and of notice-and-choice, and in 2016 she served as chief technologist at the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.
fieldFixes.influence: Her post-mortem is a detailed insider's account of why P3P failed: the negotiation protocol was dropped, Internet Explorer's use of compact policies as a cookie gate led thousands of sites to post copied or erroneous policies, and no enforcement followed — lessons W3C itself repeated when it declared P3P obsolete in 2018.
fieldFixes.thread: P3P's founding idea was a browser that would 'negotiate with websites, and take actions on their users’ behalf' — the idea that person-proffered terms (IEEE 7012) and AI agents now revive. The difference is who states the terms: in P3P the site published its policy and the person's browser evaluated it; in IEEE 7012 the person proffers the terms.

issues: The influence field is wrong on two points. (1) It says 'The single browser header he prototyped ... became the Do Not Track signal later standardised at W3C'. Soghoian and Stamm's 2009 prototype sent two headers, 'X-Behavioral-Ad-Opt-Out: 1' and 'X-Do-Not-Track: 1'. The W3C Note's acknowledgements say 'The DNT header field is based on the original Do Not Track submission by Jonathan Mayer (Stanford), Arvind Narayanan (Stanford), and Sid Stamm (Mozilla)', not on Soghoian's add-on. (2) 'Standardised' overstates the outcome: the work never became a W3C Recommendation and ended as a Working Group Note. Soghoian's own post says only that in 2010 'the header I had implemented and lobbied for somehow managed to catch the attention of' advocates, regulators and browser vendors, and that 'focus has shifted to a single header'. fieldFixes.influence: The browser-header approach he prototyped and pitched in 2009 resurfaced in 2010, when the FTC chairman revived talk of Do Not Track; the single DNT header that W3C's Tracking Protection Working Group later took up was based on a submission by Jonathan Mayer, Arvind Narayanan and Sid Stamm. fieldFixes.contribution: In 1995 the Ontario privacy commissioner's office, where Cavoukian was then assistant commissioner, co-published with the Dutch data-protection authority (the Registratiekamer) the report 'Privacy-enhancing technologies: the path to anonymity', which proposed a user-controlled 'identity protector'. She developed Privacy by Design from the 1990s and, as Ontario's commissioner, set it out in 2009 as seven principles — among them privacy as the default setting and 'Respect for User Privacy — Keep it User-Centric'. In October 2010 the world's data-protection commissioners, meeting in Jerusalem, adopted a resolution recognising Privacy by Design. Her 2014 report with Daniel Castro defending de-identification was sharply disputed by Arvind Narayanan and Edward Felten.

fieldFixes.contribution: Kaliya Young, known online as 'Identity Woman', co-founded the Internet Identity Workshop, first held in Berkeley in October 2005, and still convenes it twice a year, now at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View. The workshop's founding question, in her words, was how individuals could own their own digital identifiers rather than live 'underneath the platforms'. She later championed self-sovereign identity — decentralised identifiers, verifiable credentials and personal agents under the individual's control — and wrote 'The Domains of Identity' (2020).
